articles.title: President Trump: Forget the midterms and finish the job in Iran
articles.summary: The war will only end by returning to the first objective Trump dropped from his list: the collapse of the fanatical, barbaric Tehran regime.
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance and Iran would like Americans to blame the war and Israel for the Republicans’ midterm electoral drubbing. President Trump, however, disagrees . He should rise above this noise and refocus on the U.S. national interest by fulfilling his repeated vow to “ finish the job ” with Iran.

In announcing Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, Trump articulated five key American goals: “destroy their missiles,” “annihilate their Navy,” “ensure the regime’s terrorist proxies can no longer destabilize the region or the world,” “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon” and “unleash [Iran’s] prosperous and glorious future.”

These original objectives have been pared back over time. The first to fall away, almost immediately, was Trump’s directive to the Iranian people to “take over your government.” By April, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine no longer mentioned ending Iran’s support for terrorism.

Trump walked back the goal of destroying Iran’s projectile threat, suggesting in June that “missiles aren’t the problem.” And, most recently, Vance put an end to demanding the end of Iran’s nuclear program, asking only for a “meaningful” reduction in enrichment.

All that remains of the original U.S. war aims is annihilating Iran’s navy, which is both already accomplished and largely irrelevant to Iran’s threat.

Operation Epic Fury has notched significant accomplishments. Trump overstates the case when he claims that Iran has “been systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially,” but seriously damaged would be correct. Iran’s nuclear program and defense industrial base still lie under rubble. Its economic lifeblood, oil exports, has been largely choked off. A whole tier of military and civilian leaders was eliminated.

Iran rebuilt its conventional military capabilities far quicker than expected after last year’s 12-Day War and could do so again. While most of Iran’s 60 percent enriched uranium was entombed by U.S. B-2 bombers, Iran still could access it. The U.S. and Israel reportedly had a plan to get it out, using ground forces, but Trump opted against it . Pickaxe Mountain, dangerous because of how deeply buried it is, was not even targeted either in last year’s war or this year’s.

Rather than be forced back into conflict by a rearmed Iran, the U.S. and Israel can and should, as Trump has said, finish the job by returning to and fulfilling his original five objectives. That means the U.S. and Israel need to soon launch a new, short but intense campaign of strikes against Iran’s remaining missile and drone facilities, coastal radars, batteries, small boat launches and air defenses.

This operation should also set the conditions for rendering inoperable Iran’s nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, and eliminating its 60 percent enriched uranium, with a ground operation as necessary. U.S. strikes should also target a portion of Iran’s domestic energy infrastructure, further weakening the regime’s hold on power, and clearly signal that Iranian retaliation will prompt further such strikes.

Such a campaign will entail risks. U.S. forces and our Israeli and Arab allies’ homelands will come under Iranian fire. Fuel prices will likely spike, at least temporarily. But the alternative, leaving the Iranian threat in place, is riskier and costlier still.

But Iran’s missiles, drones, proxies, navy and nukes are not the primary threats. Even if they were fully destroyed, Iran would attempt to rebuild them or find new means of aggression. The threat is the Iranian regime and its determination to destroy America, Israel and the West at any cost. Thus, even a new round of strikes will not finish the job. The U.S. will have to remain vigilant, monitoring Iran and potentially returning for additional strikes to stop it from reconstituting.

The war will only end by returning to the first objective Trump dropped from his list: the collapse of the fanatical, barbaric Tehran regime. No deal should be made with Iran; it would only sustain the regime. The U.S. military’s blockade is vital to further weakening it and accelerating its demise.

But more is needed: encouraging defections, fomenting distrust and friction among regime factions and strengthening opposition within Iran, providing everything from public statements of support to covert arms shipments to enable the Iranian people to overcome the regime’s violent forces and dispatch the Islamic Republic to the dustbin of history.

The midterms changed the political landscape in Washington but not the geopolitical chessboard in the Middle East. The Iranian threat remains; removing it is still the only way to end the war.

Michael Makovsky, Ph.D., a former Department of Defense official, is president and CEO of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America. Blaise Misztal is vice president for Policy at JINSA.

articles.title: Pope Leo hold first mass in Uruguay, urges crowd to be ‘bridge builders’
articles.summary: Vatican says some 40,000 people gathered to listen to the head of the Roman Catholic Church in western city of Paysandu.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has addressed tens of thousands of people who gathered for his first mass in western Uruguay as he continues his 12-day tour of Latin America.

The head of the Roman Catholic Church urged the crowd at Paris London Park in Paysandu on Saturday to be “bridge builders” and “share the joy” of their faith.

More than 30,000 people – many from Uruguay but also from neighbouring Argentina and Brazil – had registered in advance to attend the service, about 375km (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said another 10,000 had shown up beyond that, despite the morning rain and blustery, grey skies.

It was the first mass of Leo’s three-nation South American tour – which also includes Argentina and Peru – which had been in doubt after the 71-year-old American pope underwent lung cancer surgery last month.

The pontiff appeared to be in good health on Saturday. While flying from Rome to Montevideo, Leo told reporters his speedy recovery was due to “trusting God, good doctors, good surgeons, and overall, I think a healthy lifestyle”.

His visit to Latin America comes as the region contends with sharp political divisions, with several right-wing leaders coming to power since United States President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January last year. Bucking the trend, left-wing Brazilian President Lula da Silva was re-elected for a fourth term in office last month.

In Paysandu, Leo urged the crowd to “forward the mission of evangelisation with enthusiasm” and to be a “fraternal community that comes together and shares life, projects, dreams and hopes”.

During Saturday’s address, he also paid homage to the region’s beloved mate tea, which is regularly shared among groups who drink from the same straw in a symbolic show of community.

It “teaches us to share and be together”, the pontiff said.

Approximately 60,000 people are expected to gather for a night-time prayer vigil led by the pope in Montevideo later on Saturday.

Leo’s visit to Uruguay is the first to the country by a pope in nearly four decades.

He will head to Argentina on Sunday before finishing his tour in Peru.

During his trip to Argentina, the pope will address President Javier Milei, a strong proponent of free markets and a close ally of US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: A Texas lawyer lost his licence in 2018 and later sued other law firms for fees from seven client cases; a November 5 appeals court reopened the dispute, finding insufficient evidence to support the firms' defence
articles.summary: Losing a professional licence does not necessarily mean losing the right to payment for work already completed.
articles.body: Losing a professional licence does not necessarily mean losing the right to payment for work already completed. That question became central to a legal dispute involving a former Texas attorney who sought fees and expenses from other law firms for seven client cases he had referred to them while he was still licensed. The firms argued that paying him after his disbarment would violate professional conduct rules and a Texas Supreme Court order. A lower court accepted their position, dismissing his claims, but an appeals court has now found that the evidence did not establish the firms' defence.In its November 5, 2026, opinion in R Kent Livesay and The Law Office of R Kent Livesay, PC v. Kaster, Lynch, Farrar & Ball, LLP, the Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals reversed the summary judgment in favour of the law firms and sent the case back for further proceedings. The ruling, available on Justia under docket number 14-25-00393-CV, did not establish that Livesay was entitled to the disputed money. Instead, the court concluded that the firms had not produced sufficient evidence to prove that his recovery was legally barred or that he had failed to complete his responsibilities before his licence was suspended.How the fee dispute beganThe dispute involved R Kent Livesay and his professional corporation, the Law Office of R Kent Livesay, PC. Before losing his licence, Livesay had referred personal injury cases to Kaster, Lynch, Farrar & Ball, LLP and Farrar & Ball, LLP. Under the arrangements, he said he had agreed to share responsibility for representing the clients alongside the firms.Livesay sent letters to the firms on December 30, 2016, stating that he could no longer represent the affected clients. His licence was suspended in January 2017 and later revoked by the Texas Supreme Court on July 6, 2018. The firms subsequently entered into new representation agreements directly with those clients, removing Livesay from their representation.In 2022, Livesay filed a lawsuit seeking payment for seven client matters. His claims included breach of contract, quantum meruit, money had and received, unjust enrichment, constructive trust and breach of fiduciary duty. He also sought a declaratory judgment concerning his right to collect fees and expenses, as well as reimbursement of expenses he said he had incurred while working on the cases. The firms denied that he was entitled to the money. They argued that he had not completed his responsibilities before losing his licence and that paying him would violate professional conduct rules and the Texas Supreme Court's revocation order.Why the lower court dismissed his claimsIn October 2024, the firms filed a motion for summary judgment seeking dismissal of Livesay's claims. They relied partly on an affidavit from Kyle Farrar, a founding partner, stating that settlement checks for the disputed cases had not been issued until after Livesay's suspension or disbarment. The trial court granted the motion in April 2025 and issued a final judgment in December 2025 in favour of the firms. Livesay appealed, arguing that the firms had not provided sufficient evidence to establish that he was legally barred from receiving the fees and expenses.A central issue was whether a disbarred attorney could still receive payment for work completed while legally practising. The appeals court referred to earlier Texas decisions, including Lee v. Cherry, which recognised that an attorney who completed the required legal work before being suspended or disbarred could still recover an agreed referral fee. However, the court also considered Royden v. Ardoin, which established that disbarment before completing a contingent-fee agreement could amount to voluntary abandonment, preventing the attorney from recovering payment for unfinished work.Texas's fee-sharing rules also require lawyers to provide proportional professional services or assume joint responsibility for the representation, along with obtaining the client's written consent. Livesay maintained that he had accepted joint responsibility for the cases, making the question of whether he completed his obligations before his licence was suspended important to the dispute.Why the appeals court reopened the caseThe appellate judges found a significant problem with the evidence submitted by the firms. Livesay had objected to Farrar's affidavit, arguing that it did not explain how he personally knew when the settlement checks were issued. Although Farrar identified himself as a founding partner, the affidavit did not establish that he handled the firms' client accounts, signed the settlement checks or otherwise had direct knowledge of the relevant transactions. The appeals court concluded that his position alone was insufficient to establish personal knowledge. It therefore ruled that the affidavit could not serve as competent summary-judgment evidence.Without that affidavit, the remaining evidence did not conclusively establish when the clients received their settlement payments. This date mattered because the firms needed to demonstrate that the client matters had concluded after Livesay could no longer continue his joint responsibilities. The court also rejected the argument that the Texas Supreme Court's revocation order automatically prevented Livesay from receiving any payment. It explained that the order did not override existing Texas law allowing disbarred attorneys to recover fees earned on matters completed while they were licensed.The November 5 decision reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings. However, the appeals court did not rule that Livesay had completed all his responsibilities or that the firms owed him the disputed fees. His entitlement to reimbursement of expenses also remains unresolved. The ruling therefore gives Livesay another opportunity to pursue his claims, but it does not guarantee that he will recover the fees or expenses he is seeking.

articles.title: Jelly Roll returned to the juvenile centre in Nashville where he spent his teenage years; he is supporting an initiative to build a 14-acre youth campus on the site
articles.summary: Country music star Jelly Roll has returned to the juvenile detention centre where he spent much of his teenage years, this time supporting an initiative
articles.body: Country music star Jelly Roll has returned to the juvenile detention centre where he spent much of his teenage years, this time supporting an initiative designed to give young people a better chance at life. The singer, whose real name is Jason Bradley DeFord, joined Nashville officials in August 2024 to break ground on a new youth campus. Planned across 14 acres, the development aims to replace outdated juvenile justice facilities with a more supportive environment for children and families. For Jelly Roll, the project is particularly personal, transforming a difficult chapter of his life into an opportunity to help others.Jelly Roll returns to juvenile centre to support Nashville's youthJelly Roll's involvement in Nashville's youth campus project carries considerable personal significance. According to PEOPLE, the musician spent several years at the Davidson County Juvenile Justice Centre during his adolescence, celebrating his 14th, 15th and 16th birthdays there. At 17, he was charged as an adult and left the juvenile facility behind.His return on August 8, 2024, marked a striking change in circumstances. Instead of arriving as a teenager facing the justice system, he attended the groundbreaking ceremony as a successful musician and advocate for young people.The News International reported that Jelly Roll wanted the new development to offer children an experience different from the one he remembered. He emphasised the importance of creating surroundings where young people feel supported rather than simply confined. His own journey from incarceration to musical success has become an important part of his efforts to encourage young people to believe in the possibility of change.Why Nashville is replacing its existing juvenile justice centreThe new Nashville Youth Campus for Empowerment, known as NYCE, is being developed to address the limitations of the city's existing juvenile justice infrastructure.According to the Juvenile Court Clerk of Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson County, the current Juvenile Justice Centre at 100 Woodland Street opened in 1994. As the city's juvenile justice system expanded, additional courtrooms and judicial officers placed increasing pressure on the available space.The expansion forced other programmes and agencies to relocate to accommodate courtroom requirements. The facility also faced infrastructure difficulties, including plumbing problems between 2019 and 2020.A master planning process identified the need for significantly more space to meet juvenile justice requirements through 2035. A 2017 plan recommended a campus-style development that could accommodate court operations and additional services without the limitations of the existing building.The proposed replacement is intended to improve both the physical environment and the way young people and their families experience the justice system.What will be provided at the 14-acre Nashville youth campusThe NYCE Campus is planned for Brick Church Pike on a 14-acre site formerly occupied by the Al Menah Shrine Temple. The location was selected for its accessibility, nearby community organisations, public transport connections and space for outdoor areas.The campus will house Davidson County Juvenile Court alongside a pre-trial housing facility for young people involved in the justice system. It is also expected to include a 24-hour assessment centre for children experiencing crises.Additional facilities will provide space for court hearings, private meetings and conversations involving families, lawyers, community organisations and court officials. A safe exchange facility is planned to support therapeutic visits between children and their parents or caregivers.Green spaces and courtyards are also part of the design, helping create a calmer environment for children and families dealing with difficult circumstances.Jelly Roll is using music to give young people another chanceJelly Roll's support for Nashville's youth extends beyond the new campus. His earlier contribution to the juvenile detention centre helped establish a recording studio for young people interested in music.PEOPLE reported that the studio, donated by the singer, opened in May 2024. The initiative was inspired by his own experience of discovering music during incarceration.For Jelly Roll, songwriting and recording became important outlets during difficult periods of his life. The studio was intended to give young people opportunities to explore their creativity and develop their musical interests while in detention. His involvement in the campus project builds on the same belief that access to constructive activities and support can make a difference in young people's lives.The Nashville Youth Campus for Empowerment is expected to become a major investment in the city's juvenile justice system. articles.title: Why do Americans keep killing each other?
articles.summary: Writer John Mac Ghlionn argues that America’s pervasive culture of violence and lethal aggression stems from deep-seated systemic issues, including extreme political polarization, socioeconomic insecurity, and a lack of a social safety net.
articles.body:
Researchers at the University of Lincoln recently found that everyday aggression (e.g., minor physical altercations) and lethal aggression do not lie on the same continuum. In other words, killing isn’t merely aggression turned up to its highest setting.

That is the theory. Then there is America, where a violent crime occurs every few seconds, and someone is shot roughly every 30 minutes.

It remains remarkably easy for most of those living in American cities and towns to stroll directly into licensed gun stores and walk out with high-powered rifles or shiny new handguns.

Background checks can be avoided for private sales in some states. And even where regulatory frameworks are formally robust, the act of owning firearms remains far less culturally stigmatized than in any other developed nation. In the U.S., guns are routinely marketed and purchased as ordinary consumer goods, sitting alongside hunting boots and camping coolers on the glass display counter at a local retailer.

It is all rather insane but also undeniably true.

When confronting the perennial question of why deadly violence runs so completely rampant across the U.S., various observers inevitably argue that Americans have simply always been an innately violent people. These commentators claim that the nation’s rugged pioneer history and wild frontier heritage actively demand widespread firearm ownership while glorifying vigilante justice — an ingrained cultural disposition toward fistfights and fatal retribution that will inevitably persist for as long as the republic itself survives.

Yet guns, and the pervasive culture of physical violence more broadly, operate merely as visible symptoms of a deeper underlying affliction. Millions of everyday Americans have absolute contempt for supporters of opposing political parties. Massive swathes of the population now view a MAGA supporter or a Gavin Newsom fan through a lens of such visceral vitriol that planting a campaign sign in one’s front yard becomes immediate ammunition for bitter, lifelong neighborhood rivalries.

Americans treat one another with extraordinary cruelty. This hyper-individualistic society has convinced the masses that financial prosperity is the single most important metric of human existence, and that falling short financially is an unmistakable indictment of a person’s moral character.

Socioeconomic success and failure are continually reinterpreted across the culture as direct reflections of an individual’s work ethic, character, raw intelligence, and basic humanity. It is deemed fundamentally uncool to be poor, precisely because remaining poor carries the implicit cultural accusation that you have somehow failed or screwed up along the way.

In many other developed countries across the globe, losing your job is painful but rarely world-shattering. In the U.S., it can become an existential catastrophe. European nations, to take a familiar point of comparison, systematically guarantee comprehensive medical care and generous unemployment benefits. They often subsidize public housing for particularly disadvantaged citizens.

In America, losing your primary employment often means instantaneously forfeiting your family’s health insurance coverage as well. This is one reason the modest household savings of the newly unemployed are unlikely to last long.

Americans treat personal finances with such desperate, suffocating solemnity precisely because the social safety net is virtually nonexistent. Lose your steady job, and you may very well lose the roof over your head soon after. Consequently, a minor fender bender or an unfairly punitive restaurant review that threatens your small business’s livelihood becomes an entirely rational cause for sudden panic. It is hardly surprising that Americans navigate daily interactions with crippling anxiety and defensive hostility.

Absent structural guarantees, practically any unexpected life event can trigger complete ruin, leaving even routine, everyday human encounters feeling like a high-stakes gamble.

For laborers, the prevailing economic model demands maximum uninterrupted output while ruthlessly penalizing any sign of physical or emotional vulnerability. Taking time off for personal wellness or to care for sick children is viewed with suspicion. Genuine job security remains entirely elusive even after years of loyal service.

Public infrastructure has decayed to the point that the working poor must shell out hundreds of earned dollars every month just for the basic privilege of driving a car to work. Should the monthly bills go unpaid because a job was abruptly eliminated, the local eviction courts process and discard impoverished families with ruthless efficiency, leaving their meager personal belongings to decorate the public sidewalks shortly thereafter.

When everyday life is an exercise in perpetual panic, and tempers remain paper-thin, it’s hardly surprising that so many people instinctively reach for a lethal weapon to settle a matter. It has become terrifyingly easy to cross a line that should never be crossed. As more people lose their jobs and their homes , we should expect more Americans to lose their minds and more to lose their lives.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Bill Maher warns Democrats that some on far-left want 'communism' after midterm sweep
articles.summary: Bill Maher told his "Real Time" audience that far-left Democrats "want communism" and urged moderates to use their midterm wins to reclaim the party.
articles.body: Comedian Bill Maher doubled down on his criticism of democratic socialists Friday, telling his "Real Time" audience that "these people want communism" and urging moderates to reclaim control of the party following Democrats' historic sweep in this week's midterm elections. On Friday, Maher spoke with writer and podcast host Coleman Hughes regarding the rise of socialist policies within the Democratic Party — and the party’s apparent appetite for more moderate candidates — during the show’s roundtable discussion. "My issues are high rents and crime," Hughes said. "Socialists don't tend to be good on those issues because they institute policies like rent control, which sound good and then end up increasing the rents in the long run." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' "And we got a hundred years of data on socialism," Hughes added. "It's not good for the economy. It's not a new idea." Maher appeared to agree with his guest, arguing that many of the policies pushed by socialist candidates are more closely aligned with communist ideology. LIBERAL HOT SPOT RESIDENTS CAN’T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS AS FAR-LEFT MOVEMENTS GAINS STEAM "We already have a lot of socialism and a lot of it is appropriate," Maher said. "That's not what these people are selling, these far-left people." Maher said some government services and programs — including Medicare, the Marine Corps and Social Security — fall under his definition of socialism. TRUMP'S CORPORATE STAKES ARE A GIFT TO THE NEXT DEMOCRATIC PRESIDENT "It's anything the government does and the private sector doesn't," the comedian said. "You just read what they say in their manifesto. They want the government to take over everything. That is a prescription for failure." Maher also argued that the sweeping victories by moderate Democrats could indicate a broader voter rejection of the policies advocated by far-left candidates. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI "To me, one of the great results of this election was it gave moderates a big stick to beat them off with," Maher told his audience. He added that moderate Democrats could use their midterm victories to regain control of the party, while suggesting that the socialist agenda may not be as popular with voters as its supporters believe. JOE MANCHIN WARNS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE GAINING GROUND AS DEMOCRATS REMAIN SILENT "Who has the guts to say this is the Democratic Party, you are doing a whole different thing," he continued. "We already have a lot of socialism, and I'm for most of it. We need most of it, but these people want communism." BILL MAHER WARNS THAT THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS BEING 'COLONIZED' BY SOCIALISTS, SAYS HIS 'VOTE IS IN PLAY' The liberal comedian has repeatedly criticized the rise of socialism within the Democratic Party and warned about socialist policies ahead of the midterms earlier this year. "I did say that it was about two months ago, and you see how quickly the news changes in just two months, because that was before the Supreme Court made a ruling on voting rights," Maher said at an event in June, referencing the Supreme Court's April 29 decision in "Louisiana v. Callais," which found that Louisiana's revised congressional map constituted an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. "So, that has changed just in the last two months, and then the Democrats just elected three very far-left democratic socialists in New York who are crazy — like outright really crazy — so like, how are they gonna blow it? I don't know, but they seem to be well on their way," he added at the time. Maher’s comments come after Democrats have won at least 254 U.S. House of Representatives races, according to the Associated Press — subsequently giving the party its largest House majority since 2009. MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER Additionally, democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass earlier this week, becoming another democratic socialist elected to lead a major American city, following New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last year. However, Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that Maher's criticisms of socialist policies — and his characterization of candidates who support them — are misguided as the comedian continues to criticize Democrats. "There is something perfectly ‘Bill Maher’ about declaring it an ‘indictment of our educational system’ that young people supposedly do not understand socialism, and then immediately revealing that he does not understand it either," Shroff said. "Medicare and Social Security are social insurance programs. The Marine Corps is literally a branch of the military." BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "If every service the government provides counts as socialism, then courts, cops and Congress are socialist too and the word has basically lost all meaning," he added. "He is mocking other people for being uneducated on the subject while demonstrating the same sloppy understanding himself." Shroff also pointed to Maher's history of dining with President Donald Trump at the White House — most recently last month — and accused the liberal comedian of criticizing socialist policies more harshly when Democrats embrace them. "And if Maher really wants to worry about socialism, he might want to look a little harder at his dinner buddy Donald Trump," Shroff said. "Trump’s government has taken roughly a 10 percent stake in Intel and about a 15 percent stake in MP Materials. Those examples are far closer to socialism than Medicare is. Yet somehow Maher’s socialism panic gets a lot quieter when Trump is the one doing it." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Fox News Digital reached out to Maher for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title: Yemeni gov’t forces report advances as Houthis say deadly strikes hit Sanaa
articles.summary: Civilians bear the brunt of fighting as 27 people reported killed in strikes on a village in Sanaa province.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces say they have repelled Houthi assaults in Marib, as the armed group said strikes on a village in Sanaa province had killed at least 27 people.

In a statement on Saturday, government forces said troops backed by warplanes and drones had fought for hours to halt Houthi advances in Marib province, destroying fortifications and combat equipment.

It said troops were also pushing into Houthi-held areas of al-Jawf province, where fighting entered a third consecutive day as part of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation launched more than a month ago by the internationally recognised government, to take control of territory from Houthi fighters.

In a separate statement, government forces spokesman, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the army had carried out 875 attacks on Houthi positions on Saturday, “neutralising” about 130 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroying or disabling 50 vehicles and missile launchers.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.

Also on Saturday, a series of strikes killed at least 27 people and wounded about 30 others in Sanaa province, the Houthi-run ⁠Saba news ⁠agency reported.

Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Sanaa-based Ministry of Health, said the attacks struck al-Shariya village, north of the capital. He said most of the casualties were women and children.

The Iran-backed Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – blamed the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government forces for the attack. The President of the armed group’s Supreme Political Council, Field Marshal Mahdi al-Mashat, vowed to “avenge” the attack.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government have not commented on the reported strikes.

The incident comes a day after the Houthis and Yemen’s government traded blame over a separate attack that killed civilians at a market in Taiz.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the Houthis put the civilian death toll from the past two days at 55, blaming Saudi air strikes, while Yemeni government officials have held the Houthis responsible for most of the casualties.

“Two narratives are blaming each other and pointing the finger at each other, while this is taking a toll on civilian casualties,” Mawry said.

As fighting continues in Yemen, the Houthis separately claimed to have launched six attacks on Saudi targets using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, but did not say when the attacks were carried out.

The group said it had targeted King Khalid international airport and oil facilities in Riyadh, an oil site in Khurais, an oil pumping station in Dawadmi, a National Guard camp in Najran and what it described as Saudi troop gatherings in Yemen’s al-Jawf and Marib provinces.

Colonel Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-backed coalition supporting Yemen’s government forces, said early on Saturday that they had shot down a Houthi ballistic missile over the Riyadh region.

articles.title: Malaysian king warns against defying house arrest order for ex-PM Najib
articles.summary: Attorney general postponed Najib Razak’s transfer from jail after court cleared him for house arrest on Friday.
articles.body:
Malaysia’s king has warned that any attempt to challenge his order granting jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak house arrest could amount to defying ⁠his decree, a day after authorities delayed Najib’s transfer.

The 73-year-old Najib was jailed for his role in one of the largest-ever global plunders of a sovereign wealth fund, the now-defunct 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).

But King Sultan Ibrahim granted him a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to serve out the rest of his sentence at home provided he paid a $12m fine.

On Friday, the country’s attorney general blocked the former prime minister’s transfer to house arrest after the fine was paid, saying his office needed more clarification on the pardon.

The king said on Saturday there was nothing to clarify, calling the pardon “clear, evident and without any ambiguity”.

“There should be no confusion in interpretation,” King Ibrahim said in a statement, adding it was not tied to any other cases against the former leader.

“Given that all conditions in the conditional pardon order have been fulfilled, any argument questioning the order leads towards denying the order of His Majesty the King.”

Najib’s lawyers thanked the monarch on Saturday, saying there was “no basis” for authorities to keep Najib in prison “a moment longer”.

“They must transfer him immediately to his residence at Jalan Langgak Duta to serve his house arrest, as His Majesty has ordered,” lawyer Farhan Shafee said in a statement.

The Attorney General’s Office issued its own statement shortly afterwards, denying it was challenging the king’s authority while giving no indication if it intended to immediately release Najib.

“This step is not aimed at delaying or denying the implementation of the Conditional Pardon Order, but to avoid any conflict in the implementation of the orders in force and to ensure no sentence is implemented unlawfully,” it said.

Hours later, the prime minister’s office said the attorney general was seeking an audience with the king to “seek pardon” and express an intent to comply, while insisting that legal questions remained that only a court could decide.

The house arrest order applies only to Najib’s first conviction.

He faces ⁠an additional 15 years in prison after being found guilty last year in another 1MDB-linked case, with the sentence set to begin after his stint in ⁠house arrest ends. Najib is appealing the verdict.

The king, a position held in rotation by Malaysia’s nine regional sultans, plays a largely ceremonial role but has the authority to grant pardons ‌under ‌discretionary powers granted by Malaysia’s constitution.

Malaysians hold the monarch and the country’s other sultans in deep respect. Negative remarks about the royalty can be prosecuted under the colonial-era Sedition Act.

articles.title: In setback to Netanyahu, rival Eisenkot to be tasked with forming next Israeli government. But the path remains complicated
articles.summary: In a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his main rival will be tasked with forming the next Israeli government, placing him one step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving leader, even as the path remains complicated.
articles.body: In a setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his main rival will be tasked with forming the next Israeli government, placing him one step closer to ousting Israel’s longest-serving leader, even as the path remains complicated. Gadi Eisenkot, a retired military chief who led the centrist Yashar party in the October 27 election, will have up to six weeks to try and assemble a coalition to replace Netanyahu. But his path to power is fraught with political obstacles and divisions within the opposition itself. President Isaac Herzog will officially give Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, his office said in a statement. Herzog’s decision followed two days of consultations last week with all parties elected to the Knesset. Eisenkot secured the support of 67 members of the incoming Knesset, including 19 from the two Arab parties. Netanyahu received just 46 recommendations. A notable crack in his once-loyal bloc was exposed during the consultations when United Torah Judaism, a traditional Netanyahu ally, declined to recommend him. Yet Herzog’s decision does not automatically remove Netanyahu from power. Eisenkot has a mandate and a parliamentary majority on paper, but not yet a governing coalition. Eisenkot is pushing to form what he calls a “national emergency government” and to swear in a minority government as soon as possible. It would comprise the four Jewish opposition parties, which together hold 48 seats: his own Yashar; Together, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. He has set four conditions for joining: recognizing Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state, commitment to the values of the Declaration of Independence, universal service – whether military, national, or civilian – and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization. The last condition effectively rules out the Arab parties from sitting in the Cabinet. But they could still support the government from outside, providing a parliamentary safety net. Israeli law requires only a simple majority to establish a government. Removing one is far more difficult, requires an absolute majority of 61 votes who support an alternative government. (The Knesset has 120 seats.) Eisenkot’s central obstacle is Avigdor Liberman. The Yisrael Beitenu leader and, at different times, former defense, foreign affairs and finance minister, has ruled out any government dependent on the Arab parties. A minority government, he argues, will be short-lived, and in the long run, will only strengthen Netanyahu. “We’ll have Netanyahu come back with 70 seats for another four years, and from there it’s a short road to annihilation,” Liberman wrote on X on Friday. Instead, Liberman proposed a different route. Dropping his years-long veto on the ultra-Orthodox parties, he urged to make a “maximum effort” to form a coalition of 61 lawmakers with the two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, and without the Joint List and Ra’am. Once it is formed, he added, three or four lawmakers from the Likud may defect. That plan, however, clashes with one of the opposition’s core commitments: to end the blanket draft exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from mandatory military service. The ultra-Orthodox parties are pressing for legislation that would enshrine the exemption, and Eisenkot, Liberman and the rest of the opposition pledged universal service throughout the campaign. Moreover, one of the ultra-Orthodox parties remains loyal to Netanyahu. Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority, is also applying heavy pressure against any Jewish-Arab political cooperation. He is challenging the election results and claims the vote was “stolen” by Arab parties by bribery and foreign funding. David Zini, his loyalist Shin Bet director, has been pushing to investigate Arab politicians without any public evidence. In a video statement Saturday, Netanyahu warned that if a minority government is formed with the Arab parties’ support, Israel will “simply not survive.” Instead, he called for a national unity government with his entire bloc, which includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. Netanyahu called for “all Zionist parties that want to preserve our one and only state of the Jewish people.” Eisenkot dismissed his message as a “pathetic spin.” In a statement, the Yashar party said, “If the Likud wants a broad unity government, it is more than welcome to announce the dissolution of the alliance with the extremists and enter a government under Prime Minister Eisenkot.” Eisenkot’s first test comes Tuesday with the swearing in of the new Knesset. The opposition intends to replace Netanyahu’s Knesset speaker, weakening his grip on power and allowing the opposition parties to begin taking some actions, such as forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas. Starting Sunday, Eisenkot will have 28 days to negotiate with other parties over Cabinet posts, budgets and policies, with a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate passes to Netanyahu for another four weeks. Eisenkot said on Friday he intends to form a government as quickly as possible, framing the moment as a national emergency. “A situation in which a caretaker prime minister in the minority, who has lost the trust of the people in such an extreme way, continues to operate the security system and law enforcement authorities, is a dangerous situation that must not continue even for one more day,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: What is Diwali, the Festival of Lights, and how is it celebrated?
articles.summary: Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and widely marked by prayers, family gatherings and the lighting of fireworks.
articles.body: Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and widely marked by prayers, family gatherings and the lighting of fireworks. More than one billion people across faiths celebrate it in the world’s most populous nation and its diaspora. The name Diwali comes from “Deepavali,” meaning “a row of lights.” Celebrants place rows of traditional clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8. The victory of light over darkness While Diwali is a major religious festival for Hindus, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Its origin stories vary by region but share a theme: the victory of good over evil. In southern India, Diwali celebrates Lord Krishna’s victory over the demon Naraka, who is said to have imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. In northern India, it honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife, Sita, and his brother, Lakshmana, after 14 years of exile in the forest. Lights, fireworks and feasting Traditions vary by region but commonly include lights, fireworks, feasting, new clothes and prayers. In southern India, many people take an early morning bath with warm oil to symbolize bathing in the holy River Ganges for physical and spiritual purification. In the north, worship centers on the goddess Lakshmi, who symbolizes wealth and prosperity. Gambling is a popular tradition, reflecting a belief that those who gamble on Diwali night will prosper throughout the year. Many people buy gold on Dhanteras, the first day of the festival, believing it will bring good luck. Other traditions include setting off firecrackers and exchanging sweets and gifts with friends and family. Celebrations also feature rangoli — geometric and floral patterns drawn on the floor with colorful powders. Other faiths’ traditions Jains observe Diwali as the day Lord Mahavira, the last of their great teachers, attained nirvana, or liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, which overlaps with Diwali, to commemorate the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment under the Mughal emperor Jahangir. Some Buddhists mark the day as the anniversary of Emperor Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism in the third century B.C. Celebrations across North America in 2026 Disney World in Florida held several days of Diwali festivities ahead of the holiday, featuring more than 500 dancers. Diwali at Times Square marked its 11th year in New York City with international performers, cultural bazaars and a lighting countdown at the Ball Drop Tower. Other community events across North America include Diwali Eve on the Waterfront in Jersey City, Diwali Family Cruise Lights on the Hudson in New York, Diwali on the Bay in San Francisco and a Diwali Fusion Bollywood Boat Party in Vancouver, British Columbia. Last year, California became the third U.S. state to make Diwali an official state holiday.

articles.title: Rebuilding US foreign policy after Trump
articles.summary: Following a stinging defeat for Republicans in the midterm elections driven by opposition to the Iran war and tariff policies, the incoming Congress is expected to attempt to restrain or reverse several of President Trump’s foreign policy initiatives.
articles.body:
The American people have spoken and issued a stinging repudiation of the Trump administration in the midterm elections.

Already, Vice President JD Vance has laid blame for his party’s poor performance on two areas of foreign policy, the Iran war and its Israel policy. Wider issues of affordability and the Trump administration’s policy on tariffs also likely loomed large in voters’ decisions.

Since returning to office, President Trump and the vocal advocates of his “America First” agenda have dominated the foreign policy debate. Ironically, part of Trump’s legacy will be the weakening of American support for policies that he pursued — from tariffs to risky military interventions — making it less likely that future presidents will pursue them. But some of Trump’s policies will nevertheless be hard to reverse, and repairing the damage will be a multi-presidential effort.

While both Trump and former President Joe Biden were willing to increase tariffs on Chinese imports, the second Trump administration took the extraordinary step on “Liberation Day” of imposing tariffs on allies and rivals alike. Trump also further unnerved close allies by talking up territorial acquisition of Greenland and even making Canada the 51st state. Wavering support by President Trump for Ukraine in its fight to ward off Russian aggression, along with antagonism to NATO, has further accentuated a rupture in long-standing U.S. support for its European allies. The Trump administration’s elimination of the U.S. Agency for International Development also flew in the face of America’s established role as the leading provider of humanitarian and foreign assistance.

Many of these foreign policy choices are unlikely to endure. The inflationary effects of rising gas prices and the unpopular war of choice against Iran led to an electoral wipeout for Republicans in the midterms. It is hard to imagine another president imposing tariffs indiscriminately as the Trump administration has done, particularly on close trading partners like Canada and the European Union. The increasing competitive threat of China’s exports in areas like critical minerals, batteries and autos is not a problem the United States can address on its own.

Moreover, there is limited domestic support for key aspects of Trump’s foreign policy agenda, including tariffs, territorial expansion, the NATO alliance, and Ukraine, according to recent surveys of the American public and U.S. foreign policy leaders conducted by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs.

The American public is only fitfully preoccupied by foreign policy, but after major policy failures like the Iran war, the American people have reacted by punishing leaders or their political parties. While the current moment may be dominated by affordability and domestic politics, choices made on foreign policy — on tariffs and Iran — loomed large in the midterms. Current international policy failures suggest another disciplining moment is likely.

With the Congress flipping after the midterm elections, we are likely to see efforts to restrain or reverse some of Trump’s foreign policy excesses. At the very least, Congress will likely use its oversight functions to hold the administration’s foreign policy architects to account, including beginning impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Congress may also move to more vigorously restrict presidential leeway regarding the use of tariffs and to ensure that the executive branch respects Congress’ appropriations power over foreign aid. This week’s rebuke of the Trump administration at the very least will also increase pressure on the administration to end the Iran war.

Having said that, some areas of Trump’s foreign policy will be difficult to undo in the short run. Simply returning to the pre-Trump internationalist status quo of support for free trade and democracy, multilateral alliances, and freedom of navigation on the high seas is not an option either. Too much damage has been done.

Reconstituting funding for foreign aid programs will also be politically fraught, as Republican voters and Republican foreign policy leaders remain hostile to many types of foreign assistance, though are more open to humanitarian assistance. On immigration and climate change, too, there are wide partisan differences both among voters and leaders, suggesting that policy debates may devolve into partisan feuds.

It won’t be easy to rebuild the foundations of U.S. foreign policy after a second Trump presidency. The legacy effects of another forever war may sap Americans’ willingness to remain engaged in the Middle East, with the Strait of Hormuz constantly threatened by a strengthened Iran. Russia’s war with Ukraine appears no closer to an end, though President Trump has tried to tilt the balance towards Russia.

On China, the American default has been a reflexive hawkishness, but other countries are loath to choose between the U.S. and its major rival. Meanwhile, the American public (and U.S. munitions) may be in no shape to prepare for another conflict.

In this context, American leaders will have to articulate at home why engagement with the world is important and what it should look like. Internationally, greater consistency and collaboration with allies will be essential to begin to gain back the trust of America’s long-standing partners, but it will take more than four years before America is once again more admired than feared across much of the world.

Jonathan Monten is associate professor in the Department of Political Science at University College London. Jordan Tama is a professor in the Department of Foreign Policy and Global Security at American University and senior nonresident fellow at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs. Joshua Busby is a professor in the LBJ School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin and senior nonresident fellow at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs.

articles.title: Hasan Piker's political rise takes centre stage as Twitch broadcast beats ABC, CBS in live viewership
articles.summary: Hasan Piker is becoming one of the biggest online voices in American politics.
articles.body: Hasan Piker is becoming one of the biggest online voices in American politics. The left-wing political streamer attracted 241,783 viewers at the same time during his election-night broadcast on Twitch as Americans followed the 2026 midterm results. His audience was nearly three times larger than ABC News' YouTube coverage and five times that of CBS News. The numbers show how political livestreamers are reaching people who might not turn to traditional news channels. Piker's growing audience also raises questions about how much influence online creators now have over American politics.Hasan Piker's 241,783 Live Viewers Put His Twitch Coverage Ahead of Major News NetworksPiker's election-night numbers were among the biggest for an individual creator covering the November 3 midterm elections. According to Streams Charts, his Twitch broadcast collected 1.75 million hours of viewing. It was the second-most-watched individual broadcast of the night, behind NBC News' coverage featuring Steve Kornacki.NBC's nearly 11-hour stream, called the "Kornacki Cam," attracted 29 million views across platforms and reached more than 300,000 viewers at its peak. Still, Piker's numbers stood out when compared with other major news networks' online coverage.His Twitch audience was almost three times the size of ABC News' YouTube audience and five times that of CBS News. However, traditional television remained much bigger overall. According to Nielsen data, NBC averaged 6.8 million primetime viewers, while ABC had 5.1 million and Fox News attracted around 4 million.The figures show that livestreamers are becoming a serious part of election coverage, even though they have not replaced television news.The wider trend was also visible across online platforms. Streams Charts reported that election-related livestreams collected 10.27 million hours of viewing across more than 2,500 channels in the 30 days before the election. That was 4.5 times the viewing recorded before the 2022 midterms.Piker alone accounted for nearly 45% of that viewing time, showing just how much attention one political creator can attract.Hasan Piker's Political Work Is Drawing Attention From Democratic CandidatesPiker's role in American politics goes beyond covering election results. He has also supported Democratic candidates and taken part in their campaigns. During the 2026 election cycle, he campaigned with Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar and backed progressive candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier. Both won congressional seats in the November 3 elections.His connection with Democratic politicians was also visible on election night. California Congressman Ro Khanna appeared on Piker's livestream. Politicians are increasingly interested in reaching people through online creators, particularly younger Americans who may not follow traditional news broadcasts.A 2025 survey by the Pew Research Center found that 38% of Americans aged 18 to 29 regularly get news from social media influencers. Among Americans aged 65 and older, that number was just 8%.This gap helps explain why political figures are paying more attention to platforms such as Twitch and YouTube. A livestream also gives viewers a chance to ask questions and respond while the discussion is happening. Unlike a regular television broadcast, the conversation does not have to stop when the news segment ends.Piker explained this difference in an interview with Reuters. He said his broadcasts involve constant back-and-forth conversations with viewers. He also described his influence as modest among Democrats under 45 who feel frustrated with the party.However, his growing role has not come without criticism. His past remarks have drawn strong reactions, including comments about the September 11 attacks. Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers also used Piker's remarks against Abdul El-Sayed during the campaign.El-Sayed had earlier asked Piker to be more careful with his comments after the streamer made remarks about the safety of Jews who supported Israel, CNN reported.Despite the criticism, Piker remains an important voice among left-wing online audiences. However, his popularity does not automatically mean he speaks for the entire Democratic Party. EMarketer analyst Max Willens told Reuters that Piker may be one of the leading voices on the far left, but comparing his influence with that of the wider Democratic Party would be going too far.For now, his election-night audience offers a clear example of how Americans are finding new ways to follow politics outside traditional television news.You use AI every day. articles.title: School aide who briefly served as NYPD officer arrested in fatal stabbing of Brooklyn jogger
articles.summary: A public school employee who briefly served as an NYPD officer has been charged with second-degree murder in the fatal stabbing of a 28-year-old female jogger in Brooklyn last week, an apparently random attack.
articles.body: A public school employee who briefly served as an NYPD officer has been charged with second-degree murder in the fatal stabbing of a 28-year-old female jogger in Brooklyn last week, an apparently random attack. Sayed Mohassib, 27, was arrested Saturday in the death of Katie Suarez, who was attacked Oct. 30 on the Belt Parkway bike path. Mohassib told investigators he had been walking along the path with a knife, police said. He told investigators he blacked out and was covered in blood when he regained awareness, according to law enforcement sources. Suarez was stabbed at least two times in the neck and was rushed to the hospital, where she succumbed to her injuries days later. Detectives used surveillance footage from the area to help identify Mohassib as a suspect. Security cameras also captured him dumping bags of garbage near his home the night of the killing. A search was underway at a sanitation facility for any evidence that may have been discarded. Mohassib spent about a month with the NYPD beginning in October 2022 before asking to be reassigned to the military, where he was removed because of mental health issues, according to a law enforcement source familiar with his background. In January 2023, the NYPD denied his request to be reinstated. The source said he was taken to the psychiatric ward at Bellevue Hospital after exhibiting strange behavior when he tried to get his job back in person. Mohassib most recently worked for the New York City Department of Education as a paraprofessional at P.S. 200, an elementary school in Brooklyn. He continued to report to work after the stabbing, law enforcement officials said. It was not immediately clear whether his psychiatric history was reviewed before he was hired. “The safety of our students is our very top priority. We have suspended this individual and will move to terminate employment pending the outcome of the conviction,” a DOE spokesperson said in a statement. “We are supporting the NYPD in their investigation however is needed.” Police believe the attack was random. Suarez was supposed to meet her parents after her run. When she never arrived, her father went looking for her and found her. She fought for her life in the hospital for several days before dying of her injuries, her mother, Yasira Suarez, said.

articles.title: More than 140,000 rally as new protests against rising costs sweep France
articles.summary: Tear gas fired in Paris and Lyon as interior minister warns authorities are ‘ready and waiting’ for rioters and looters.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across France for a fourth consecutive weekend, in another show of anger against the government.

About 146,000 people rallied across the country to protest against the rising cost of living on Saturday, including 46,000 in Paris, the Ministry of the Interior said.

Unions put the figure at 250,000 protesters nationwide, with 75,000 in the capital.

The demonstrations come just days after an estimated 575,000 people took part in a rally organised by trade unions.

About 70,000 security personnel were deployed across the country on Saturday, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warning that authorities would be “ready and waiting” for anyone engaging in rioting or looting.

Clashes broke out between police and some protesters in the capital, Paris, despite a lower turnout than in previous weeks.

Footage posted online by the CLPRESS news agency showed police charging at protesters and using tear gas in an attempt to disperse the crowds. A police officer was also seen hitting a protester with a baton.

Police said a group of 200 individuals attacked officers as they were arresting a man who had set fire to a rubbish bin in a square in Paris, the AFP news agency reported.

In the southeastern city of Lyon, police also fired tear gas to disperse several hundred people in the city centre who were blocking a road during an unauthorised gathering.

Reporting from the French capital, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said people working in a variety of jobs attended Saturday’s demonstrations in support of the student-led movement.

“I spoke to one railway worker who told me it was really important to be here today. He said not only was it important to protest against the cost of living, but that it was also important to support young people,” Butler said.

“There is no doubt that the trade unions, who’ve been weakened in recent years, really feel there is a sense of momentum,” she said. “Many of the workers that I’ve been speaking to say this is their time to really press the government for higher salaries and better facilities.”

The demonstrations in France began in September over poor conditions and a lack of resources at French high schools. The protests later expanded to encompass a host of grievances, linked to worsening living standards. The movement continues to be led by France’s students, but people of all ages have been taking part.

This weekend’s protests take place against the backdrop of France’s upcoming presidential election, due to be held in April. Polls put far-right candidate Marine Le Pen of the National Rally first, followed by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party.

Melenchon unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters and promised to do the opposite of incumbent President Emmanuel Macron.

He pledged to stimulate the economy by capitalising on consumer spending and “through billions [of euros] that already exist”, adding that these savings “must be channelled towards our country’s ecological and social needs”.

articles.body: Donald Trump was caught unawares by Vice President JD Vance's detailed analysis of the midterm defeat and in fact he was angry, Laura Loomer has claimed. The far-right activist, who took a break from hosting her podcast after the GOP's rout, said she was told this by a White House official. A day later, Susie Wiles was fired.Vance said the party lost the election because of the war. He said voters who had supported Trump and him in 2024 had switched to Democrats because they wanted the administration to end the war, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first and reconsider the US relationship with Israel.“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote. He also questioned whether continuing the conflict had been worth the political cost of losing Republican control of the Senate.When Trump reacted to the analysis, he attempted a balance. He did not undermine JD Vance and partly agreed with JD's takeaway but he also added that he would do it again even if he is electorally hurt because in the long run Iran can't have a nuclear weapon."It’s been brought to my attention by a WH official that President Trump was actually blindsided by the statement made about the Iran war the day after the election. He didn’t approve the statement and no, he wasn’t happy about it, despite how it’s being presented to the public. I’m told he was quite angry about it," Loomer said."It’s very interesting how there’s an entire ecosystem of people who have been brought in to force you to believe he approves of a statement that undermines his agenda. I don’t think it’s the last we will hear of it," Loomer added.JD Vance's 614-word statement blaming war that apparently did not have Trump's approvalOne of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true.But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:1) End the war2) Focus on cost of living/inflation3) Put America First4) Change our relationship to IsraelOur voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.I remain hopeful about our country. articles.title: In 2002, Ray Charles promised seven children $500,000 trusts in exchange for waiving further inheritance claims; 24 years later, his foundation's $3.5 million lawsuit over 51 songs resurfaces
articles.summary: Legendary American singer Ray Charles' complicated family legacy has resurfaced following renewed attention to a legal battle involving seven of his
articles.body: Legendary American singer Ray Charles' complicated family legacy has resurfaced following renewed attention to a legal battle involving seven of his children and the rights to 51 of his musical compositions. In December 2002, Charles reportedly promised seven of his adult children irrevocable trusts worth $500,000 each, on the condition that they agreed not to pursue further inheritance claims against his estate. The arrangement became contentious after his death in 2004, when the children attempted to reclaim copyright interests in songs written or co-written by their father. The Ray Charles Foundation subsequently filed a lawsuit seeking at least $3.5 million, arguing that the copyright claims violated the agreements they had signed. The dispute involved multiple court proceedings and raised questions about the rights of artists' heirs under US copyright law.Ray Charles' $500,000 inheritance agreement with seven childrenAccording to the foundation's lawsuit, Charles informed all 12 of his adult children in 2002 that he intended to establish irrevocable trusts worth $500,000 for each of them if they agreed to waive further claims against his estate.The written agreements stated that the trusts would represent their entire inheritance and that they would not seek any additional share of their father's estate. The foundation's complaint maintained that the arrangement was intended to provide financial security to the children while allowing Charles to direct his remaining estate towards charitable causes.All seven children involved in the subsequent lawsuit signed agreements acknowledging the arrangement. According to the court records, each of them eventually received the promised $500,000 trust.Charles died in June 2004, aged 73. His will named the Ray Charles Foundation as the sole beneficiary of his estate, including his rights under music-related contracts.Why Ray Charles' children sought rights to 51 songsThe disagreement emerged in March 2010, when seven of Charles' children served copyright termination notices on music publishers covering 51 musical compositions written or co-written by their father.The children relied on provisions of the US Copyright Act that allow authors or certain qualifying heirs to terminate earlier copyright transfers after specified periods. These provisions can enable copyright interests to return to the author or eligible heirs, subject to statutory conditions.The seven children filed 39 termination notices covering the 51 compositions. The notices proposed different effective dates, ranging from April 1, 2012, to September 28, 2019.The foundation challenged the notices, arguing that they violated the inheritance agreements and could undermine its rights to royalties from Charles' music. It also questioned whether the compositions qualified for copyright termination, maintaining that some had been created under work-for-hire arrangements.The dispute was therefore not simply about receiving another inheritance. It concerned whether the children could legally reclaim copyright interests in their father's music despite the agreements they had signed.Famous songs included in the copyright disputeThe 51 compositions included several recognisable songs from Charles' career, particularly works he created during the 1950s.Some of the titles specifically identified in the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals' judgment include:I Got a WomanA Fool for YouBlackjackLeave My Woman AloneHallelujah, I Love Her SoMary AnnWhat'd I SayThe dispute concerns the underlying musical compositions and their publishing copyrights, rather than simply ownership of the original sound recordings. This distinction matters because a song's composition and its recorded performance can have separate copyright ownership.Why the Ray Charles Foundation sought $3.5 millionThe foundation filed its lawsuit in March 2012, accusing the seven children of breaching their written agreements with their father by attempting to reclaim copyright interests in the disputed compositions.It sought at least $500,000 from each of the seven defendants, bringing its total damages demand to $3.5 million.The foundation also requested a court order preventing the children from claiming ownership of the disputed copyrights, transferring those interests to other parties or exploiting the compositions without the necessary permissions.It argued that the copyright notices threatened its ability to receive royalties from Charles' music, which formed an important source of funding for its charitable activities.The legal battle over copyright inheritanceThe case raised questions about Sections 203 and 304(c) of the US Copyright Act, which provide mechanisms for terminating certain copyright transfers after specified periods.These provisions allow authors or qualifying heirs to reclaim some rights previously transferred to publishers, subject to statutory conditions and exceptions.The foundation challenged the children's notices on several grounds. One of its arguments was that certain compositions had been created under work-for-hire arrangements, which could make them ineligible for copyright termination.The case initially faced a setback in January 2013, when a federal district court dismissed the foundation's federal claim and struck its state-law claims under California's anti-SLAPP legislation.However, the foundation appealed. On July 31, 2015, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the dismissal of the federal claim and sent the case back to the lower court for further proceedings.The appeals court ruled that the foundation had sufficient legal standing to challenge the termination notices because the potential loss of copyright-related royalties could affect its financial interests.The decision did not establish that the children had violated their inheritance agreements or that the foundation was entitled to the $3.5 million it demanded. It addressed whether the organisation had the legal right to pursue its challenge.Ray Charles Foundation ordered to pay seven children $89,000 in legal feesThe litigation also produced a financial setback for the foundation. In an earlier district-court ruling, US District Judge Audrey Collins ordered the organisation to pay approximately $89,000 in attorneys' fees to the seven children after they successfully challenged its claims.The children had persuaded the court to dismiss the foundation's federal claim and strike its state-law claims under California's anti-SLAPP law, which protects certain activities involving the exercise of legal and constitutional rights.The foundation objected to the legal-fee calculation, arguing that the children's lawyers had reconstructed their working hours rather than maintaining contemporaneous records. However, the judge found the submitted declarations sufficiently reliable to establish the reasonableness of the fees.The legal-fee award arose from the earlier district-court proceedings and should be distinguished from the Ninth Circuit's subsequent 2015 decision, which revived the foundation's federal challenge.Who was Ray Charles?Ray Charles Robinson, popularly known as Ray Charles, was an American singer, songwriter and pianist widely regarded as one of the pioneers of soul music. Born on September 23, 1930, in Albany, Georgia, he lost his eyesight during childhood and became blind by the age of seven.He rose to international prominence by combining gospel, rhythm and blues, jazz and country influences. His best-known songs include Georgia on My Mind, Hit the Road Jack, Unchain My Heart and What'd I Say.During his career, Charles received 17 Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1986. He died on June 10, 2004, aged 73, at his home in Beverly Hills, California.He had 12 children, and his estate plan placed significant emphasis on continuing his charitable work through the Ray Charles Foundation.What does the Ray Charles Foundation do?Established by Charles during his lifetime, the Ray Charles Foundation supports scientific, educational and charitable initiatives. Its work includes providing research and scholarship grants benefiting people who are deaf, blind and underprivileged young people.The organisation was intended to continue Charles' philanthropic interests after his death. It relies on royalties generated through the commercial use of his musical works to support its activities.The foundation's interest in the 51 compositions was therefore connected to its ability to generate royalty income and use those funds for charitable programmes.You use AI every day. articles.summary: New Zealand's centre-right governing coalition has a path to return to power after taking a narrow lead in a closely fought election.
articles.body: New Zealand's centre-right governing coalition has a path to return to power after taking a narrow lead in a closely fought election. With 97% of the vote counted early Sunday, National Party and its allies the libertarian ACT party and the nationalist New Zealand First party have 67 seats between them, enough to govern in a 130-seat parliament. But that small majority could yet be overturned when special ballots are counted, and the opposition hasn't conceded defeat."It is heartening to see that on the numbers so far, National is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said.One of the big stories of the night was the rise of the centrist Opportunity Party, which will enter parliament for the first time and could end up holding the balance of power once the final result is known at the end of the month.You use AI every day.
