articles.title: Arch Manning, Texas escape Missouri after wild officiating controversy sends SEC showdown into chaos
articles.summary: Texas Longhorns escaped Columbia after Arch Manning's controversial fumble ruling and a chaotic SEC officiating crew left Missouri fans stunned.
articles.body: The argument of whether Texas would make the college football playoff if it were to lose another game this season will have to wait another week. But, that doesn’t mean the controversy surrounding this Longhorns squad is going away any time soon after the 34-20 win over Missouri. Did SEC officials get together before the game and decide that pure chaos was on the agenda for this showdown at Missouri? CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Besides the fact that there were multiple calls that went against Missouri, some reasonable, I don't think we've seen this much madness in one football game this season. Everything came to a head in the third quarter, as Arch Manning was hit from behind while trying to also complete a pass. The Texas quarterback was obviously trying to pass the football, while at the same time a Missouri defender got his hand on the ball. The problem was that Manning's arm was moving forward, even with the ball tipped by a Missouri defender. Then, as the ball laid on the ground 12 yards ahead of the the line of scrimmage, a Texas receiver picked up the football, while trying to snag it before a Missouri defender fell on the ball. According to the SEC officiating crew, the call on the field was ruled a fumble. So, officials reviewed the play, which concurred within the replay center at SEC offices, where they ruled that the call on the field would stand. While a befuddled broadcast crew and those reacting on social media complained, Arch Manning dropped a dime just two plays later for the Texas touchdown that tied the game at 20-20. This was just one example that created plenty of confusion for viewers at home, while the home Missouri crowd was left stunned. We still have no idea what consistency looks like for Texas As for the game itself, outside a number of weird calls by the officiating crew, this was expected to be a tough outing for the No. 7 Longhorns against a Missouri squad led by quarterback Austin Simmons. Turns out, we got this chaotic Saturday started with a bang, as Maybe this is one of those examples of how anyone in the SEC can be beaten on any given Saturday. But there will be plenty of questions surrounding why some of these calls were made, with a Missouri team that continued to cause problems for a Longhorns squad that is still searching for a mistake-free football game this season. DID WE CREATE A MONSTER? ARCH MANNING’S ‘AW SHUCKS’ PERSONA IS GONE BEFORE MUST-WIN OLE MISS GAME Did we actually learn anything about Arch Manning's presence within the pocket? Sure, there were multiple instances of Texas looking like a squad that could be a threat if it were to make the college football playoff. But, we still saw a team led by Steve Sarkisian that is troubled by their own mistakes with penalties, while also trying to create a rushing attack without Hollywood Smothers. Texas stays alive in CFP race, but Death Valley awaits No matter how fans at home feel about the outcome, and if Texas was lucky enough to be bailed out a few times by the officiating crew, the Longhorns will gladly take this win and prepare for a showdown against LSU next week in Baton Rouge. YES, THE SEC IS STILL GETTING RIDICULOUS PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN THE AP TOP 25 POLL The win over No. 19 Missouri will obviously sit well with the CFP rankings committee if Texas were to catch a loss that would put them at three on the season. But, it's clear that Steve Sarkisian is learning a few new things about his redzone offense, even if some of the field position was handed to them on a silver platter against the Tigers on Saturday. articles.title: Israeli president picks Netanyahu’s rival Eisenkot to form new government
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has selected Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival, to try to form a new government following the parliamentary elections last month. Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority in the Oct. 27 elections, and no party received enough seats in the Knesset for a governing majority. The president of Israel has…
articles.body:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has selected Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival, to try to form a new government following the parliamentary elections last month.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority in the Oct. 27 elections, and no party received enough seats in the Knesset for a governing majority.

The president of Israel has the authority to choose which party leader has the ability to form a government, a decision partially informed by the preference of Knesset members. Most members said they preferred Eisenkot, and he now has 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of an additional 14-day extension.

Still, while the Arab parties’ members said they preferred Eisenkot, they may not necessarily agree to join his party’s governing coalition. Eisenkot put out four principles that anyone joining his coalition must agree to, including labeling Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Building a coalition with those principles appears to be difficult. The head of Ra’am, an Arab party, said he would not label Hamas a terrorist organization. And if Eisenkot does get the Arab parties to join his coalition, he may lose the support of Yisrael Beiteinu, a right-wing party, whose leader endorsed Eisenkot but said his party would not be in a government with Arab parties.

The opposition leader joined Netanyahu’s emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, but later resigned over disagreements about the direction of the war.

Eisenkot’s son and nephew died in Gaza while fighting Hamas in the war, and he remains opposed to the creation of a Palestinian state. He is hawkish on Iran and supports Israeli military action against Hezbollah in Lebanon.

President Trump endorsed Netanyahu for reelection just ahead of the vote in Israel, a significant show of support for a pair of world leaders that have at times sharply disagreed about foreign policy.

Back in June, Trump called Netanyahu “f—king crazy” over the country’s escalating operations in Lebanon. And on Election Day Trump said the U.S. would cut off $4 billion in aid to Israel, saying Netanyahu agreed to it.

articles.title: Venice was built on more than 100 small islands in a marshy lagoon, with its buildings resting on millions of wooden piles driven into the mud; kept underwater and away from oxygen, many have survived for centuries
articles.summary: We imagine walking on water, how would it feel? How would it feel to have water instead of a solid ground below your house?
articles.body: We imagine walking on water, how would it feel? How would it feel to have water instead of a solid ground below your house? While Kashmiri houseboats and Maldivian water cottages can provide you a preview, an entire centuries old city still seems unimaginable. The renowned city of Venice has actually survived on water with innovative upside down forest design. The city is a unique experience where the streets are waterways, boats replace buses, and centuries-old palaces seem to rise straight out of the sea. The city has been a source of curiosity for travellers, architects, engineers, archeologists among others. And, studies on the floating city have revealed interesting facts.A city built where land meets waterBefore being intricately planned, Venice developed across more than a hundred small islands in the Venetian Lagoon. These consisted of shallow waters, mudflats and marshy ground with connection to the Adriatic Sea. Located in northeastern Italy, the lagoon actually proved to be a safe haven against the invading forces of the time. The arrangement worked for temporary refuge but the people wanted to extend their imagination to build a permanent settlement. However the challenge was that how could anyone construct sturdy homes, churches and palaces on ground that seemed barely capable of supporting them?This challenge was overcome by using the landscape to the advantage of engineering innovation. The builders discovered that the soft lagoon soil can be strengthened by driving wooden poles deep into the ground, packing them closely together and creating a firm platform on which to build. Over generations, this technique transformed an apparently unsuitable stretch of marshland into one of Europe's most extraordinary historic cities.The forest beneath the streetsUnexplored is the story behind the forest that lies below the streets and palaces of Venice. The foundations beneath Venice were made using timber from trees such as alder, oak, larch, pine and elm. Workers known as battipali hammered these poles into the ground by hand, sometimes singing rhythmic songs to coordinate their labour. There were ancient songs in praise of Venice, its republican glory, its Catholic faith, and declare death to the enemy of the time, the Turks. Even today a Venetian expression na testa da bater pai (literally 'a head that is good to pound down the piles') is used even today to say that someone is dull or slow-witted.Even the scale of the operation is surprising. The foundations of the Rialto Bridge alone contain approximately 14,000 tightly packed wooden poles, while around 10,000 oak trees support the Basilica of San Marco. The construction process was remarkably precise. Workers drove wooden piles deep into the lagoon bed until they could go no further, starting from the outer edges and gradually moving towards the centre. These poles were usually arranged in a spiral pattern, with approximately nine piles packed into every square metre. Once firmly in place, their tops were cut to create an even surface below sea level. Thick wooden zatteroni (boards) or madieri (beams) were then laid across them, forming a sturdy base for the stone structures above. Oak was later used exclusively for ship building which eventually made it too precious to bury in the mud.Why doesn’t the wood simply rot?Normally, wood exposed to moisture eventually deteriorates. So how have these foundations survived for hundreds of years? The unusual conditions that have sustained beneath the city are to be credited for this wonder. The oxygen is scarce underneath where the wooden piles remain submerged in waterlogged soil. This limits the activity of fungi and other organisms that would otherwise break down the timber much more quickly. The wood does not become immortal, however, bacteria can still cause deterioration.Moreover, water intrudes in spaces within the wood where bacterial activity has damaged the wooden structures. This also helps the timber in retaining its shape. Meanwhile, the historically placed compact soil and tightly arranged piles continue to support the buildings.Venice's wooden foundations are not indestructible. Some structures have even gradually settled over the centuries. The city now faces newer challenges associated with flooding, rising sea levels and the preservation of its historic architecture. Yet its foundations remain an inspirational reflection of how much ancient builders achieved with the materials available to them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: NZ election: Can a new government win over disillusioned voters?
articles.summary: Polling shows the mood among Kiwis is low, with faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the main parties at the polls.
articles.body:
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.

"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."

"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.

"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confessed. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explained, declining to chat further.

"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.

But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.

More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.

Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.

A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.

Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.

But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.

"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."

It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.

But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.

New Zealand hasn't always felt like this.

For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey – literally – for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.

A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends – which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life – were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.

"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics, tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."

Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's dive really accelerated during the Covid pandemic.

Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.

Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.

But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.

"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.

Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.

The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.

"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"

Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home, and high inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.

The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.

And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.

"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.

Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities.

"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.

This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.

Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and their parents have considered moving to Australia.

"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.

There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.

At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Fielding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton, an agricultural worker of 30 years, says last year was the best he's had.

The cattle industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.

He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.

"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'

"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."

Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.

But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.

"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.

Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young poeple - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, while attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.

Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.

"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

The transformation former Labour PM Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 was never realised, while her achievements have been wound back by her successors.

Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation .

The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.

"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."

National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi – protest march – led by Māori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.

There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.

Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control – such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.

But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."

No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.

"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says, adding with a wry smile: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

articles.title: Despite warnings from Trump admin, after the ‘Blue Wave’ many migrants bound for the US are hopeful
articles.summary: Two days after Democrats routed Republicans in the US midterm elections, the American Embassy in El Salvador posted a stern reminder on social media.
articles.body: Two days after Democrats routed Republicans in the US midterm elections, the American Embassy in El Salvador posted a stern reminder on social media. “U.S. immigration laws remain in effect,” the Spanish-language post read. “The midterm election results do not represent changes to current immigration policies.” Nevertheless, the Democratic “Blue Wave” appears to have encouraged some migrants to undertake a risky journey to the US. The hope for an easier passage to the United States was especially palpable this week among a pair of migrant caravans bound from Honduras and El Salvador. Some told CNN that with the imminent Democratic majority in Congress, they are betting it will be easier to reach the United States. All asked to remain anonymous due to the dangers associated with embarking on the journey to the border. “That’s the hope,” said Beatriz M., who is traveling with her husband and her 9- and 11-year-old children from El Salvador, “that we can make it to where we’re going.” Beatriz and dozens of other Salvadorans set out on Friday from the Western Bus Terminal in San Salvador for Tecún Umán, on the Guatemala-Mexico border. “This is not the usual flow of passengers,” a bus company employee told CNN, asking not to be identified because he was not authorized to speak publicly. Upon arriving in Tecún Umán, the group intends to join up with other migrants, among them the caravan that left Honduras on Election Day and is already making its way through Guatemala. Southwest border encounters fell sharply after US President Donald Trump took office in 2025, tightening controls at the border with Mexico and initiating a wave of deportations to halt an “invasion” of migrants into the United States. Some in the caravans gathering this week hope that after the elections, migrants might receive better treatment at the hands of US immigration officials. Many have made the journey before, including Santiago, a Honduran man who told CNN he had been deported twice from the US. “We hope that with this change everything will improve for us,” Santiago said of the US midterm results. Juan, a Honduran who lived in the US for 26 years and was deported on September 15, joined the caravan in Honduras after learning about it through social media. “After I was deported in September, I tried to enter again twice, but they sent me back from Mexico,” said Juan. “I found out about this caravan online and I’ll try one more time, to see if I can get into the United States, because my wife and two children are there.” “Not enough to get by” Not all migrants share optimism that the election results will ensure a warmer welcome at the US border. At a border crossing in Guatemala, a man named Aníbal told CNN that whichever party is in charge in the US, entering illegally often ends in deportation. “Nothing has changed,” Aníbal said. “Democrats and Republicans are the same, so if they capture us tomorrow, we’ll just head there again.” “Let’s see who gets tired first,” he added. “Them or us.” For numerous migrants who spoke to CNN, the risk of deportation is outweighed by the crush of poverty in their native countries, and the painful distance from relatives who managed to stay in the US. “I have my family over there, and here there’s no work,” said Carlos E., a Salvadoran who left via bus on Friday for the Guatemala-Mexico border. “I’ve been unemployed for four months, and that’s what motivated me to want to hit the road.” José Q. is also seeking to reunite with his family. “I haven’t seen them in two years,” he told CNN just before boarding a bus. He said he’d just finished a video call with his loved ones to let them know he was about to begin the journey and that he hopes to hug them soon. “The truth is there’s work here, but it’s not enough to get by,” Mauricio S., a young farmer, told CNN. When he found out a group was leaving from El Salvador, he decided to join, hopeful — like everyone else making the trip — that he will have a chance to better his lot and help his family. “The situation in the United States hasn’t been easy, but the idea is to try our luck,” Mauricio said.
